oneliner.t: Five-term Republican U.S. senator from Maine (since 1997) and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, seeking a sixth term against Democrat Troy Jackson on Nov. 3, 2026.

upbringing.t: Collins is one of six children of Donald and Patricia Collins, who both served as mayor of Caribou; her father, a World War II veteran, served in the Maine House and Senate. The family runs S. W. Collins, a lumber and hardware business founded by an ancestor in 1844 and now led by her brother. Her uncle Samuel W. Collins Jr. sat on the Maine Supreme Judicial Court (1988–1994). She graduated from Caribou High School in 1971 and took part in the U.S. Senate Youth Program that year, then earned a B.A. in government from St. Lawrence University (1975), magna cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa.

education.deg: B.A. Government (magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa)

career.role: Legislative assistant to Rep./Sen. William Cohen; staff director, Senate Oversight of Government Management Subcommittee (1981–1987)
Commissioner, Professional and Financial Regulation (appointed by Gov. John McKernan)
New England regional director (appointed by President George H. W. Bush)
Founding executive director, Center for Family Business
U.S. Senator from Maine; Appropriations chair since Jan. 2025; former chair of Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (2003–2007) and Aging (2015–2021)

platform.t: Argues her seniority (which she says rose from 99th to 7th) and Appropriations chairmanship let her deliver federal money to Maine; her first general-election ad featured her advocacy for $6 million toward the Eastport Breakwater.
Disputes that she votes with Trump 96% of the time, citing a roughly 70% figure; said she is 'not exactly his favorite senator.'
Calls herself the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada and cites a tariff exemption for Canadian road salt.
Says she voted to assert Congress's war-powers authority; voted against early war-powers resolutions, then backed ending the war after the April 30, 2026 War Powers deadline.
Says ICE needs reforms but that disbanding it would undermine deportation and drug enforcement; says the ICE share of the 2026 DHS money was about half of $70 billion over four years.
Says she disagrees with the overturning of Roe v. Wade; stands by her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.
Describes herself as a strong supporter of Israel; asked in the Oct. 6, 2026 debate whether U.S. military funding should change, said the current level is good.
Blames Maine's high electricity rates on state legislative decisions, including Jackson's votes, rather than federal policy.

promises.t: Keep using her Appropriations chairmanship and seniority to bring federal funding to Maine (stated reason for seeking a sixth term).
Keep U.S. military funding for Israel at its current level.

said.where: official Senate bio (collins.senate.gov/about) — campaign site not reachable

record.t: Wikipedia gives the same date and place.

claims.claim: Her family's lumber business, founded in 1844, has been run by six generations.

record.t: S. W. Collins, a lumber and hardware chain, was founded in 1844 by an ancestor; her brother Samuel is president.

claims.claim: Both parents served as mayor of Caribou; her father, a WWII veteran, served in the Maine House and Senate.

record.t: Wikipedia: both parents served as mayor; Donald Collins served one term in the Maine House and four in the Maine Senate.

claims.claim: Graduated Phi Beta Kappa from St. Lawrence University in 1975.

record.t: B.A. in government, 1975, magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa.

claims.claim: Appointed Maine commissioner of professional and financial regulation (1987), SBA regional director (1992), and founding director of Husson's Center for Family Business (1994).

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same posts and years (Husson role Dec. 1994–1996), plus a 1993 stint as Massachusetts deputy state treasurer that the bio omits.

claims.claim: Has cast more than 10,000 consecutive votes — the longest perfect voting record in Senate history.

record.t: She cast her 10,000th consecutive roll-call vote in early June 2026 and has not missed a vote since 1997. Sen. William Proxmire's streak (10,252) is longer, but he had missed votes earlier in his career, so hers is the longest by a senator who never missed one.

claims.claim: In 2020 became the first Republican woman to win a fifth Senate term.

record.t: She did win a fifth term in 2020 (50.98%); no independent tally of the 'first' was checked.

claims.claim: Repeatedly ranked the most bipartisan senator by the Lugar Center and Georgetown University.

record.t: The Lugar Center index itself was not opened. Separately, Newsweek notes VoteView places her among the most centrist Republican senators in the 119th Congress.

claims.claim: She has voted nine times to end the Iran war.
claims.short: Nine votes to end Iran war

record.t: Of 14 Democratic-forced war-powers votes since February 2026, she voted against five failed resolutions, then supported ending the war after the April 30 War Powers deadline. Both her 'nine' and Jackson's 'five against' are accurate counts; PolitiFact called her count selective.

claims.claim: The 96% votes-with-Trump figure is misleading; her real figure is about 70%.

record.t: BDN found the 96% figure misleading and out of date (a CQ-Roll Call subset of bills with an explicit Trump position, 95% in the first seven months of 2025). The figure Collins cited matches a separate CQ party-unity score (just over 72% with fellow Republicans), which measures alignment with her party, not with Trump.

claims.claim: More than a third of Jackson's bills died after unanimous rejection in committee.

record.t: BDN's search found about 36% of the bills he led died that way over his career, but 19% in his final two years. Her companion claim of 100 vetoes of his bills was not assessed.

claims.claim: Maine has the fourth-highest electricity rates because of how Jackson voted in Augusta.

record.t: Jackson helped enact solar subsidies projected in 2023 to cost about $225 million a year, but BDN notes these are a small part of bills; natural gas (over 40% of generation) and regional pipeline limits are the commonly cited causes. The ranking itself was not verified.

claims.claim: A Biden-era federal audit found $42 million in improper payments and fraud in Maine Medicaid autism services, and Jackson did nothing.

record.t: The HHS inspector general flagged about $45.6 million as 'improper' or 'potentially improper,' not fraud, and found similar problems in other states (at least $56 million in Indiana).

claims.claim: The ICE share of the roughly $70 billion she approved was about half, over four years.

record.t: The June 2026 law allotted about $38 billion to ICE, $26 billion to CBP and $5 billion to DHS through 2029.

claims.claim: Reports that she received illegal campaign contributions are false; Martin Kao is in jail.

record.t: Kao, a Navatek executive, pleaded guilty in 2022 to an illegal conduit-contribution scheme that sent more than $200,000 to her 2020 campaign and a pro-Collins super PAC (including $150,000 via a shell LLC to 1820 PAC); he is serving an 87-month fraud sentence. Prosecutors called her 'Candidate A' and did not accuse her or her campaign of wrongdoing; her campaign said it divested the contributions. The money was illegal on the donors' side, which the denial glosses over.

claims.claim: She is the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada and secured a road-salt exemption.

record.t: 'Most outspoken' is a characterization; the road-salt exemption was not independently verified here.

claims.claim: Advocated securing $6 million to help replace the collapsed Eastport Breakwater.

record.t: No appropriations record for the breakwater money was opened in this pass.

said.t: Said she did not believe Brett Kavanaugh would overturn Roe v. Wade; says she disagrees with the decision that did.

did.t: Voted to confirm Kavanaugh, who joined the 2022 Dobbs majority overturning Roe; she says she does not regret the vote. She was the only Republican to vote against Amy Coney Barrett (Oct. 26, 2020).

saydo.topic: Medicaid cuts in the 2025 tax-and-spending law

said.t: Objected to the bill's Medicaid provisions.

did.t: Voted to advance H.R. 1 on June 29, 2025, then voted Nay on final passage (one of three Republicans); it passed 51–50 on the vice president's vote.

said.t: 'I am pro-Israel' (to Zeteo); in the Oct. 6, 2026 debate called herself a strong supporter and said the current aid level is good.

did.t: Voted against discharging resolutions to block arms sales to Israel (S.J.Res. 111, Nov. 2024; S.J.Res. 41, July 2025).

promises_prev.promise: Serve only two Senate terms (pledge made during the 1996 campaign).

evidence.t: She ran and won again in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020 and is seeking a sixth term in 2026.

complicating.t: The Wikipedia article does not say how she has explained setting the pledge aside; her stated reason for running now is her seniority.

entries.t: Said she would not vote for Trump.
Voted not guilty on both articles in the first impeachment trial.
One of seven Republicans to vote to convict in the second impeachment trial (Feb. 13, 2021).
Says she is 'not exactly his favorite senator'; sources conflict on whether Trump endorsed her.
Voted against early Democratic war-powers resolutions (five times).
After the April 30 War Powers deadline, voted to advance a resolution requiring congressional approval and kept supporting such resolutions through late September.
One of four Republicans voting Yea on cloture for S. 3385, a three-year extension (failed 51–48).
Voted Yea on cloture for H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act (all 53 Republicans Yea; cloture failed 53–47).
Voted Yea on S. 5, the Laken Riley Act (all Republicans Yea; passed 64–35).
Approved the 2026 DHS funding (about $38B for ICE through 2029); says ICE needs reform, not abolition.

donors: Out-of-state billionaires and their spouses (nearly 100, Jan. 2025–May 2026; about $9M of their ~$10M in pro-Collins giving went to Pine Tree Results)

trades.note: MarketBeat's 3-year view lists one disclosed sale, Globe Life Inc. (Aug. 5, 2024, $15,001–$50,000), without saying whose account; its header claims 420 career trades, which the table does not show. Her spokesperson says she has never bought, sold or owned individual stock as a senator and that a third-party adviser manages her husband's investments; the Maine Independent reported her husband owns Boeing and RTX stock (his holdings, not hers).

note.t: Senate eFD annual reports were not reachable from this research tool, so net worth, assets and filing timeliness are not recorded. Her husband, Thomas Daffron, was a lobbyist and COO at Jefferson Consulting Group (2006–2016) and consulted on her 1996, 2002 and 2008 campaigns.

democracy.t: Voted Nay on the objection to Ohio's electoral votes.
Voted Nay on the objection to Arizona's electoral votes.
Voted Nay on the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes.
Voted to convict Donald Trump on the article of impeachment for incitement of insurrection (one of seven Republicans).
Voted Yea on cloture for S. 5271, a federal voter photo-ID requirement (cloture failed 52–46; all Republicans Yea).

debates.note: Accepted four televised debates (Oct. 6 CBS13/FOX23, Oct. 8 WMTW, Oct. 13 WABI/WAGM, Oct. 15 News Center Maine/Press Herald/Maine Public); declined an August CNN/Bangor Daily News debate; refused town-hall formats.

townhalls.note: No public town halls documented in the sources read; her campaign says she prefers individual and small-group meetings. Jackson's claim of a '25-year streak' of avoiding town halls was not verified.

note.t: Born and raised in Caribou (1952–1971), later worked in Maine 1987–1992 and has lived there since at least 1994 (Husson College in Bangor; home in Bangor). She spent 1975–1987 on Capitol Hill and 1992–1993 in SBA and Massachusetts posts. The year count is approximate.

checks.legal: No direct CourtListener/Justia/PACER search (CourtListener and Justia were not reachable from this tool). News archives read: Civil Beat/Maine Monitor coverage of the Martin Kao case (federal court records); WRIC coverage of the Oct. 8 debate (ProPublica's Sept. 2026 Navatek contract report as summarized there). Collins was not charged, sued or accused of wrongdoing in that case. Senate Ethics Committee site not fetched; no Senate Ethics action against her appeared in the sources read.

Ad spend rankings were not available.
checks.democracy: Senate certification roll calls 2005 and 2021 (provided public records, senate.gov); second impeachment vote; 2026 voter-ID cloture vote.

recordx.note: Has not missed a roll-call vote since taking office in 1997 (10,000th consecutive vote in early June 2026; BDN dates it Thursday June 4, Scripps describes it as a Friday). Senate eFD filing timeliness and FEC notices (RFAI) for her committee could not be checked.

corp.t: Business PACs have given heavily in every cycle: about $1.07M from corporate PACs and $517K from trade-association PACs in the 2026 cycle (per donor reports into Sept. 2026), and about $6.35M corporate / $2.96M trade over her career. In 2026, America's Credit Unions (a trade group) spent about $1.56M in independent expenditures supporting her.

lobby.t: Pro-Israel PACs: AIPAC PAC $9,994 directly in the 2026 cycle, NORPAC $23,895 over her career, plus FIPAC, JACPAC, USI PAC and others (about $73K direct in total). Zeteo reported AIPAC PAC money was nearly 20% of her 2025 receipts (figure not verified). Other country-organized PACs: Iranian American PAC $10,000 (2008–2012) and New Cuba PAC $5,000 (2016).

research_notes: MONEY: FEC totals (S6ME00159, through 2026-06-30) come from the provided public-records file. 'other' = receipts minus individual, PAC and party contributions ($4.41M; probably joint-fundraising transfers, not itemized here). Wikipedia lists a higher June 30 'raised' figure ($18.93M), which likely uses a different FEC summary line; the FEC figures are used here. The Q3 report (due Oct. 15) was not yet available. The 2026 PAC-by-type breakdown comes from donor committees' own reports and runs past June 30. NRSC coordinated party expenditures for her total $3,485,443 (24C) and are not counted as receipts. The 'ideological' PAC category in the FEC organization codes includes some professional-firm PACs (e.g. Deloitte, EY), so treat the business vs. ideological split with care. Independent-expenditure figures are raw line-item sums. KEY VOTES: senate.gov roll-call pages could not be opened directly. Collins's votes on S.J.Res. 111, H.R. 23 cloture, S.J.Res. 41, S. 5271 cloture and H.R. 7008 cloture are derived from the official party totals (all Republicans voting the same way, with Collins not listed as absent) in the project's Senate key-vote file. Her H.R. 1 Nay is documented by Wikipedia and is consistent with the 50–3 Republican split, and her S. 3385 cloture Yea was confirmed from the official page in the Alaska pass. Her votes on S.Res. 852 (Israel §502B, Sept. 29, 2026; one Republican Yea) and H.Con.Res. 86 (Iran war powers, June 23, 2026; four Republican Yeas) were not individually confirmed. KAO CASE: a donor's crime is not the candidate's; no finding against Collins. RELATIVES: her husband's stock holdings are his own and are not attributed to her. OFFICE YEARS: 36 = Senate (Jan. 1997–present, ~29) + Maine commissioner (~5) + SBA (~1) + Massachusetts deputy treasurer (~1); the appointed-post dates are approximate. Photo omitted (no Wikimedia file URL opened).
